Hi Marissa —

Thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap from our side and a few clarifying questions so we can align on next steps: 

- Primary SLO: end-to-end median latency for typical user prompts should be under 250ms; 95th percentile should be < 600ms for requests up to ~200 tokens.
- Concurrency & throughput: steady-state ~60 QPS, with peaks to ~180 QPS for 5-10 minute bursts during promotions.
- Streaming: important — we want partial tokens to appear as soon as possible (users perceive latency as ~first-byte). Ideally partial streaming within 100-150ms for short prompts.
- Scale expectations: we need fast burst capacity during peaks (ability to ramp from 60 -> 180 QPS within ~2 minutes).

Can you confirm how Redwood handles warm pools, scale-up times, and queueing behavior under burst? Also attaching our rough traffic CSV and the SLO template you mentioned.

Hi Kate —

Great to chat — thanks for the clear recap and attachments. Quick answers and proposed next steps below. I copied Rishi (SE) + Vivek (AE) for technical details and commercial alignment.

Summary answers:
- Warm pools & burst: Redwood supports prewarmed GPU workers (warm pool) that can accept requests immediately. For models we recommend prewarming enough capacity to cover steady-state + a planned buffer for expected bursts.
- Scale-up times: cold scale (spin up new nodes) is typically 90-180s depending on cloud zone and GPU type; warm pool transition is < 20s for handing traffic to an already-warmed worker.
- Queueing & graceful degradation: short bursts beyond capacity will queue at the router (configurable max queue 30s) with priority for realtime/streaming routes. We also support overflow policies (route to smaller model variant or return 503) and throttling.

Action items:
1) Rishi — can you confirm the model family and recommended warm pool sizing for ShopFast (based on the traffic CSV)?
2) Kate — can you share the 95th percentile request token lengths and a sample of streaming expectations (first-byte timing you mentioned)?
3) I'll schedule a 60-min technical deep dive next week to walk through warm pools, peering, and a pilot plan (Dedicated pool + burst reservations).

Attaching our SLO template filled with default Redwood guidance — please adapt.

Hi Kate — following up with more technical detail from the SE side.

Notes:
- Model & latency: for your workload (median ~120 tokens), we typically see end-to-end median latencies ~120-220ms on x2 GPUs with streaming enabled. 95th percentile depends strongly on sequence length and batching - we can tune batching/continuous-batching windows to prioritize latency.
- Warm pool behavior: warm pools keep model weights loaded and JVM/containers ready. Hand-off from the load balancer to a warm worker is < 20s. Warm pools are the fastest way to absorb bursts.
- Cold starts: if additional nodes are required beyond the warm pool, node provisioning (cold) is ~90-180s; to reduce this we recommend: prewarmed buffer, burst reservations, or setting autoscale thresholds to keep a minimum floor.
- Queueing: Redwood routers maintain a short in-memory queue per route. Default safe queue depth is 30s; requests older than configured timeout are dropped or can be rerouted. We support priority queues for streaming routes to reduce head-of-line blocking.
- Fallbacks: when you hit capacity limits we can: a) shed to a smaller model (faster, cheaper), b) return partial results (streamed best-effort), or c) return an explicit 429/503 depending on SLA.

Sizing suggestion (starter):
- Steady-state 60 QPS -> warm pool sized for 70-80 QPS to avoid immediate queuing.
- Short bursts to 180 QPS -> reserve burst capacity for additional 120 QPS in a burst pool that can be handed traffic within 20s if prewarmed, otherwise cold scale will take 90-180s.

I'll prepare a short worksheet to show cost tradeoffs (warm pool vs reserved burst) for your traffic pattern.

- Rishi

- Promos drive the peak: typical peak windows are 5-12 minutes, we can tolerate up to ~30s queueing but prefer streaming to remain responsive to users.
- Streaming expectation: first partial token should appear within 120ms for our shortest prompts (under 50 tokens); longer prompts can stream progressively.
- Cost note: we want a pilot that limits cost with a clear rollback if SLA breaches occur.
